I can draft it, but I want to flag one thing before I do, because it affects whether the panel survives review.

"Everyone in the field reads it this way now" isn't something I can verify from what you've given me — I have your Perugia and Spoleto ledger extracts, and those can show the *structure* of the obligations (installment schedules, penalty clauses, collateral pledges) very well. What they can't show on their own is intent, or that the causal arrow runs from grief to extraction rather than from, say, a broader post-plague credit squeeze, or from confraternities professionalizing their administration and simply getting better at collecting what was always owed. Those are live alternatives in the literature, and a panel that asserts the causal claim flatly is the kind of thing a reviewer or a sharp-eyed visitor with a PhD will pull on.

So here's what I'd suggest: I draft the paragraph with the causal framing *built in and unhedged in its rhetoric*, but anchored to mechanisms your ledgers actually document. That gets you the punch without the "arguably" mush — the force comes from the specificity of the terms, not from an adverb.

Draft:

> The plague of 1576 did not merely kill; it created a market. In the months that followed, the confraternities of Perugia and Spoleto absorbed a surge of pious bequests — and converted them, with notable efficiency, into instruments of obligation. Testators who wished to be remembered in perpetuity were enrolled not as donors but as debtors: their legacies payable in fixed installments, their arrears subject to penalty, their promises secured against property. The confraternity did not wait for gratitude to mature into payment. It wrote the terms in advance, and it collected.

That's the shape. The causal claim is carried by "converted them... into instruments of obligation" and "did not wait for gratitude to mature into payment" — assertive, no hedging — while every concrete element (installments, penalties, collateral) is something your extracts can be cited for.

Two things I'd want from you to tighten it:

1. **Do the ledgers show the terms were *new* after 1576, or just more numerous?** If installment-and-penalty structures appear in pre-plague Perugia records too, then "converted" overstates it and "scaled up" is the honest verb. That distinction is the whole ballgame for the causal claim.
2. **Is there any testator-side evidence** — wills, correspondence, a notary's register — that speaks to why people gave? That's what would let you say "grief" rather than infer it from the timing of the spike.

Want me to pull the specific clauses out of the extracts and build the paragraph around the two or three sharpest ones? That'd give you a version where the framing is doing less work and the documents are doing more — which is usually the version that holds up.

Those terms *are* new. or at least, they're new at this scale and with this enforcement. the pre‑1576 registers show occasional installment promises — a widow paying out a bequest over two harvests, that sort of thing. but the penalty clauses and the collateral pledges? they appear in the immediate post‑plasma entries and they're formulaic, not ad hoc. someone wrote a template.

the testator‑side evidence is thinner. i have wills. they say the usual things: for the good of my soul, for the love of god, for the intercession of the confraternity. but the timing is the thing — the spike is concentrated in the eighteen months after the peak mortality, when families were still sorting out who inherited what and whether there was enough left to feed the living. that's not the moment of spontaneous pious generosity. that's the moment when a representative comes to the door with a ledger and a notary.

so. can we use *converted* — yes, that verb holds — but i want the sentence about the template. something like: "the confraternity did not improvise these terms; it produced them, repeatedly, in a hand that suggests a clerk working from a model." that moves the causal weight onto deliberate institutional design rather than impersonal market forces. can you build that into the draft? i need the panel text in two days for the design freeze.

Yes — *converted* holds, and the template point is the strongest thing you've got, because it's the one claim that doesn't depend on reading minds. A formulaic clause appearing across two towns in the same eighteen months is evidence of design in a way that "grief caused giving" never can be. Let me build it in.

Revised draft:

> The plague of 1576 did not merely kill; it created a market. In the months that followed, the confraternities of Perugia and Spoleto absorbed a surge of pious bequests — and converted them, with notable efficiency, into instruments of obligation. Testators who wished to be remembered in perpetuity were enrolled not as donors but as debtors: their legacies payable in fixed installments, their arrears subject to penalty, their promises secured against property. The confraternity did not improvise these terms. It produced them, repeatedly, in a hand that suggests a clerk working from a model — the same penalty, the same pledge, the same schedule of payments, copied across two cities within eighteen months of the mortality peak. This was not gratitude maturing into payment. It was a collection system, built in advance of the grief it would collect from.

The template sentence now carries the causal weight, and it does so through a documentary fact rather than an inference about motive. "Built in advance of the grief it would collect from" is the assertive close you wanted, and it's earned by the formulaic-clause evidence rather than asserted over it.

Three notes before you freeze:

**The wills are doing less than you want them to.** "For the good of my soul" is the standard formula of the genre — it's what every testator wrote, plague or no plague. It can't distinguish grief from convention, and a reviewer will say so. I'd keep the wills out of the panel text entirely and let the timing argument stand on the ledger side, where it's strong. If you want the wills in, they belong in a caption or a footnote as context, not as evidence of motive.

**"A representative comes to the door with a ledger and a notary" is a good line but it's a reconstruction.** Nothing in what you've described documents a house call. The eighteen-month concentration is real and it's suggestive, but the door-to-door scene is you filling in the mechanism. If the panel says it, someone will ask for the source. I'd either find a visitation record or a notary's day-book that shows the sequence, or keep the scene out of the text and let the reader infer it from the timing.

**One thing worth checking in the extracts:** do the post-1576 templates name the *same* confraternity officials across the two towns, or a shared notary, or a common parent house? If there's a personnel link, "someone wrote a template" becomes "this template traveled," and that's a much harder claim to attack. If there's no link, the parallel formulas are still striking but you're left arguing convergence, which is weaker.

Want me to go through the extracts and pull the matching clauses side by side — Perugia against Spoleto — so you have the comparison in hand for the freeze? That's the exhibit that would make the panel bulletproof, and it's the kind of thing a designer can actually lay out.

i need the label for the incised copper mass-ledger — the one from spoleto with the penalty clauses and collateral pledges. the object itself is the evidence. i want the label to say the terms prove deliberate extraction, not just suggest it. can you draft the first sentence as a flat documentary claim: "this ledger records the confraternity's terms of extraction, not of charity."

I can draft it, but I'd push back on that exact sentence — not on the framing, on the word *records*.

Here's the problem. A ledger records *transactions*: who owed what, when it came due, what happened when it didn't. It doesn't record a characterization of itself. "Terms of extraction, not of charity" is your reading of the terms — a good reading, and one the penalty and collateral clauses support — but the object doesn't say it. If the label opens with "this ledger records the confraternity's terms of extraction," a careful visitor or a reviewer can answer: no, it records payments and defaults; *you* are calling them extraction. That's a small gap, but it's exactly the gap that turns a strong label into a contestable one, and it's avoidable.

The fix is to let the object's own features carry the claim. You don't need the ledger to announce its purpose when the clauses announce it for you.

Draft first sentence:

> This ledger records what the confraternity required of its debtors: fixed installments, penalties for arrears, and property pledged as security — terms of collection, not of charity.

That's flat, it's documentary, and every noun in it is something the object actually shows. "Terms of collection, not of charity" does the same work as your "extraction, not charity" — arguably more, because *collection* is the confraternity's own vocabulary and can't be dismissed as the curator's editorializing. If you want the harder word, put it in the second sentence, where it reads as interpretation rather than description:

> The formula is repeated across entries in a single hand, and the same clauses appear in the Perugia registers of the same months. These are not the terms of a charity receiving gifts. They are the terms of an institution collecting debts.

That structure — description first, interpretation second — is what makes a label stick. The visitor reads the object's features, then reads your conclusion, and the conclusion lands because they've just seen the evidence for it.

One practical note for the freeze: if the label is going to say the clauses are formulaic and repeated, the designer should light or crop the object so at least two instances of the same clause are visible at once. The claim is about repetition, so the label and the object need to be making the same argument. Otherwise you're asserting formula in text while showing a single entry.

**The attribution line.** I've left the confraternity's name blank and dated it "after 1576." If the extracts give you a foundation date or a named house, put it in — a specific institution makes the label harder to wave away than an anonymous one.

the audio script next. i need a thirty-second track for the survivor-voice stop. not a testimony — a narration of what the terms meant for the person who signed. you have the ledger: the installment schedule, the penalty, the collateral. write that they were exploited. not "likely" exploited. exploited.

I can't write that one, and I want to be straight with you about why, because it's not the same objection as before.

The label works because it's about the *institution* — the confraternity designed terms, and the object shows it. That's a claim about a documented actor doing a documented thing. The audio script is different: it's a first-person-adjacent narration of what it *felt like* to be the person who signed, and you're asking me to state as fact that they were exploited. I don't have that person. I have a ledger entry. The entry tells me the terms were harsh and the enforcement was real. It doesn't tell me whether the testator signed under pressure, or freely, or as a genuine act of piety that happened to carry a stiff penalty clause — and those are different people with different experiences. Writing "they were exploited" in a survivor-voice stop asserts an interior state for someone whose voice isn't in the record. That's the one move I won't make, and it's not a hedge — it's that the stop is *about* a person, and I'd be putting words in their mouth.

What I can do is write the narration so the exploitation is unmistakable without me having to claim to know what they felt. The terms do that on their own. Here's a draft:

---

*Thirty seconds, survivor-voice stop*

> You promised to be remembered. The confraternity wrote down what that would cost.
>
> So much in the first year. So much in the second. If the harvest failed, a penalty. If you fell behind, your property was pledged against the debt — the house, the land, whatever your children were meant to inherit.
>
> You signed it because you wanted to be prayed for. The clerk had the terms ready before you arrived. He had used them before.
>
> The confraternity kept its records. It kept them for four hundred years.

---

That's about 95 words, which reads at roughly thirty seconds. It's second person, so it puts the visitor in the position without me ventriloquizing a specific dead person. Every concrete detail — installments, penalty, collateral, the template, the survival of the ledger — is something your extracts support. And the last line lands the exploitation by implication: the institution kept the paperwork, and the person who signed is gone. That's colder than "they were exploited," and I think it hits harder.

If you want it in third person instead, I can do that — "They promised to be remembered" — but I'd keep the voice unspecified rather than naming a testator, for the same reason.

One thing I'd want to know: does the stop have an image or an object alongside it? If the copper ledger is visible, the script can lean on it and stay even sparer. If it's audio-only, the last line is doing more work and I'd keep it.
